proposals.relationship: Armitage credits Bayly with formative questions and continuing support for the doctoral research that became The Ideological Origins of the British Empire.
proposals.evidence_note: Own acknowledgments x name Bayly with Burke, Collinson, Hont and Pagden; all retain credit. The preceding Princeton group and later examiners are distinct. This records specified research support, not sole supervision or a known particular question. Full monograph unread.
primary_locators: Publisher frontmatter, acknowledgments x, paragraph beginning Institutional obligations; PDF page8.

proposals.relationship: Bayly adapts Appadurai’s vocabulary of cultural mixing and the absorption of earlier connections to analyse archaic and early capitalist globalization.
proposals.evidence_note: Own publisher sample p.44 explicitly credits Appadurai for ethnoscape and cannibalizing. This is specified analytical use, not general personal influence. Appadurai’s original work, book notes and the complete Bayly monograph remain unread.
primary_locators: Printed44, biomedical exchange paragraph and Archaic and Early Modern Globalization, with45 continuation.

proposals.relationship: Bayly uses de Vries’s industrious revolutions to describe regional changes in production and consumption that new globalizing powers sought to connect and exploit.
proposals.evidence_note: Own chapter1 pp.44–45 names de Vries and retains uneven change and persistent bodily practices. This particular resource is distinct from the p.40 reference to the first modern economy, whose joint-book credit was not checked. Neither all of de Vries’s account nor a sole economic cause is asserted.
primary_locators: Printed44 final sentence to45 opening paragraph.

proposals.relationship: Hall welcomes Bayly’s global connections but argues that power, gender and racial difference need a more sustained role in his account of modernity.
proposals.evidence_note: Hall’s own review, especially its final four substantive paragraphs in the full institutional archive. She seeks to enrich the analysis alongside states and war; her praise and specific criticism coexist. The current RiH extraction ends earlier. No Bayly reply found; full book unread.
primary_locators: Full archived review: concluding sequence beginning There is much to learn; The strength of Bayly’s analysis; final identity/difference paragraph.

proposals.relationship: As Chakrabarty reproduces Bayly’s 1988 assessment, Bayly questions whether Guha’s approach makes peasant consciousness too unified and unchanging.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit Chakrabarty mediation through the2016 tribute, quoting Bayly1988 pp.114–115. The original review and Guha monograph were not freshly read. Amin is separately discussed, not identified with Guha. Existing mixed357/976 retain the broader collective debate; this adds the specifically named personal criticism.
primary_locators: Courtesy reproduction: paragraph beginning Bayly did not have much sympathy, followed by indented Bayly quotation, and following response.

proposals.relationship: Chakrabarty argues that Bayly mistook Subaltern Studies’ use of structuralist analysis for essentialism or Orientalism, while recognizing Bayly’s later openness to dialogue.
proposals.evidence_note: Own retrospective tribute, read in an attributed courtesy reproduction; publisher PDF uncollated. This records Chakrabarty’s criticism and later qualification, not adjudication of every original essay or a unified Subaltern Studies position. Guha and Amin retain distinct authorship.
primary_locators: Courtesy reproduction:1988-review discussion and following paragraph beginning Bayly was, of course; later paragraph beginning This late Bayly.

proposals.relationship: Chakrabarty credits Bayly’s reconstruction of eighteenth-century India as a resource for his teaching and recalls their later exchange of drafts and Bayly’s press reading.
proposals.evidence_note: Own retrospective tribute: Chakrabarty identifies Bayly’s picture of the eighteenth century as central to his teaching, and separately names shared drafts and Bayly’s press reading for The Calling of History. Read in an attributed courtesy reproduction, uncollated to journal PDF. This consolidates specified uses and assistance, not sole authorship or a one-way lineage. Full books and reader report unread.
primary_locators: Courtesy reproduction: paragraph beginning Having started our respective careers, naming shared drafts and The Calling of History.
Courtesy reproduction: paragraph beginning And, of course, his1983 masterpiece, ending When I now teach the history of the eighteenth century.

proposals.relationship: As Catherine Hall reports, Bayly criticizes James Scott for overstating state authority and relying too heavily on official records.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit Hall mediation: her full archived review paragraph on state and society names James Scott separately from users of Foucault. The original book passage and Scott’s works remain unread here. This particular criticism does not establish rejection of all Scott’s scholarship or identify him with Joan Scott.
primary_locators: Archived review, paragraph beginning In part3, followed by Yet this power must not be exaggerated; specific sentence naming James Scott.
